title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
hook: a street is closed with a tent, a lamp is lit, and nobody plans to sleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: Ravidas at his bench, and the Ganga in a cobbler's bowl. Which ordinary piece of work did you do slowly and well? Day one thousand four hundred eight.

Nine at night in a Punjabi neighborhood. A lane has been closed off with a bright tent. There's a stage at one end, draped in red and gold, and on it a picture of the Goddess seated on her lion. A lamp is burning in front of her. Plastic chairs fill up, then the floor fills up, aunties, kids in pajamas, uncles who said they'd stay an hour. A singer with a harmonium starts, and the whole tent answers back: Jai Mata Di. Victory to the Mother. Nobody here plans to sleep. Today, the night a Punjabi family stays awake for the Goddess.
screen: `A LANE TURNED INTO A TENT.` → `A LAMP BEFORE THE GODDESS.` → `JAI MATA DI.`

segments.voice: It's called a jagran, or in Punjabi, a jagrata. The word means a waking, a vigil. Why does a family hold one? It can be a thank-you. A child was born, a son or daughter married, a new house finished, an illness passed, a prayer answered. So the family invites the Goddess, Durga, called simply Mata, Mother, and keeps her company through the night. The lamp in front of her, the jyot, isn't allowed to go out. And what happens all night? Singers lead bhents, songs offered to the Mother, sung in Punjabi and Hindi, fast and slow, some of them about the hill shrines where her devotees climb to see her. Those shrines sit in the mountains north of the Punjab plains: Vaishno Devi in a cave, Jwalamukhi where flames burn out of the rock, Chintpurni, Naina Devi. A jagran brings a little of that mountain into a lane in the city. People dance. Kids fall asleep on laps and wake up for the loud parts. Tradition keeps a story for the last hours, the tale of a devoted queen named Tara, told as the night turns gray. Last, who it's for. The word for the night is about waking, and that's the point. Staying awake for someone is what love does: a parent with a sick child, a friend at a hospital bed. A jagran turns that kind of love toward the Mother. The family that was cared for stays up to keep her company. And the whole lane is invited. At dawn there's prasad, sweet food blessed and shared, and everyone goes home tired, and full.
screen: `JAGRAN — A WAKING, A VIGIL` · `A THANK-YOU TO THE MOTHER` · `SONGS ALL NIGHT, THE LAMP KEPT LIT` · `STAYING AWAKE IS WHAT LOVE DOES`

segments.voice: Call and answer, for two minutes. Sit, and let the breath slow. In the tent, the singer calls and the crowd answers. Let your breath do the same: the in-breath calls, the out-breath answers. Then think of someone who once stayed awake for you, or someone you stayed awake for. Let them be here in the quiet, one breath calling, one breath answering. If you pray, you can let the answer be the tent's words, Jai Mata Di, and keep the Mother company, as the jagran does. The bell holds the time.
Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, the jagran, a night awake with singing for the Mother, held in thanks, with the whole lane invited. Today's word.
Your line: Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, thank the person who once stayed awake for you, in a message, a call, or a few honest words. Day one thousand four hundred eight.

howItsDone: Punjabi Hindu families hold a jagran, or jagrata, for Mata, for instance in thanks for a blessing: singers lead devotional songs through the night before a lit jyot, and prasad is shared at dawn.
